def: Henri Fayol's framework of general management principles such as division of work and the scalar chain, focused on top-down organisational efficiency.
A corporate governance theory explaining the conflict of interest between shareholders (principals) and managers (agents), resolved through audits and performance incentives.
Fayol's principle that the power to give orders must be matched by an equal obligation to accept accountability for the outcomes.
Physical, psychological, language, cultural, perceptual, organisational or attitudinal obstacles that distort or block the transfer of a message.
A graphical representation of all combinations of two goods a consumer can purchase given a fixed income and fixed prices.
Inflation driven by a wage-price spiral, where workers and firms adjust wages and prices based on expected future inflation.
The application of moral principles to corporate conduct, balancing the profit motive with social welfare and stakeholder interests.
The point at which a consumer maximises utility subject to the budget constraint, where the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line.
A management theory holding that there is no single best way to organise; effectiveness depends on matching structure to the situation (structure, environment, technology, people).
The system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled to balance stakeholder interests.
The responsiveness of demand for one good to a price change in a related good — positive for substitutes, negative for complements.
The integration of social, environmental and economic responsibility into business operations; mandatory in India above specified net worth, turnover or profit thresholds.
The system-wide distribution of decision-making power across multiple levels of an organisation — functional, geographic, product-based or market-based.
The transfer of responsibility and decision-making power from a superior to a subordinate, while the superior retains ultimate accountability.
Inflation caused when aggregate demand in an economy exceeds aggregate supply capability.
An ethical approach focused on adherence to moral duties and principles rather than outcomes.
A slowdown in the rate of inflation, where prices continue rising but at a reduced pace.
A measure of how responsive quantity demanded is to changes in price, income, or the price of related goods.
The stage of the communication process where the sender transforms thoughts into transmittable symbols such as words, gestures or visuals.
Fayol's principle of promoting team spirit and unity to strengthen organisational cohesion.
A situation requiring a choice between two or more conflicting moral values or obligations.
Henri Fayol's foundational set of administrative principles covering organisational structure, direction, and personnel management.
A government's use of taxation and public spending to influence economic conditions such as inflation.
Communication that follows official organisational channels and hierarchy, ensuring consistency and accountability.
Taylor's concept of supervision by multiple task-specialist foremen rather than a single generalist supervisor.
A comprehensive measure of price change, calculated as the ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP, multiplied by 100.
An unofficial, informal communication network that spreads information — often rumour-based — rapidly through an organisation.
The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders, equal to Consumption + Investment + Government Expenditure + Net Exports.
Total income earned by a country's residents, both domestically and abroad, equal to GDP plus net factor income from abroad.
Elton Mayo's research proving that productivity is driven by social and psychological factors, not merely physical working conditions.
An informal organisational structure built on self-managed teams rather than traditional hierarchy.
Robert Katz's managerial skill category involving the ability to lead, motivate and resolve conflict among people.
An extreme, uncontrollable rise in prices exceeding 50% per month, typically leading to currency collapse.
The responsiveness of demand to a change in consumer income, distinguishing normal, inferior, necessity and luxury goods.
A graphical representation of all combinations of two goods that provide a consumer with the same level of satisfaction.
A persistent rise in the general price level of goods and services, resulting in a decline in purchasing power.
Unstructured, spontaneous communication such as the grapevine or face-to-face interaction that builds relationships and speeds up decisions.
Mintzberg's category of managerial roles — figurehead, leader, liaison — focused on relationships and status.
A model of oligopoly pricing where the demand curve has a kink at the prevailing price, reflecting rivals' asymmetric reactions to price changes.
The sustainable profit level a firm can earn in a given market structure — normal profit under perfect/monopolistic competition, potentially supernormal under oligopoly/monopoly.
An organisational design with dual reporting lines, combining functional and project-based authority.
Central bank actions such as adjusting interest rates or reserve ratios to control money supply and inflation.
A market structure with many sellers offering differentiated products and relatively easy entry/exit.
A market structure with a single seller, a unique product, and blocked entry, giving full control over price.
Taylor's technique of analysing worker movements to eliminate wasteful actions and set efficiency standards.
The total money value of all final goods and services produced by a country's normal residents over a year, including net factor income from abroad, measured at factor cost (NNP at factor cost).
A management theory (1920s-30s) emphasising human relations, motivation and teamwork over purely mechanical efficiency.
Any physical, psychological or semantic interference that disrupts the transmission or understanding of a message.
The minimum profit level required to keep a firm operating in an industry — the typical long-run outcome under perfect and monopolistic competition.
International corporate governance guidelines covering shareholder rights, equitable treatment, transparency and stakeholder roles.
A market structure dominated by a few large sellers with interdependent pricing decisions.
The Modern/Systems Approach view of an organisation as an interdependent set of subsystems interacting with its external environment.
Fayol's principle that resources — materials and people — should be systematically arranged in their proper place.
A visual map showing an organisation's hierarchy, roles, and reporting relationships.
Average income per person in an economy, calculated as national income divided by total population, used as a standard-of-living indicator.
A market structure with an infinite number of sellers, homogeneous products and free entry/exit.
Income actually received by individuals before direct taxes, including transfer payments but excluding retained corporate profits.
Taylor's wage system paying a higher rate per piece to workers who meet the standard output and a lower rate to those who fall short, linking pay to output.
The practice of charging different prices to different consumers or markets for the same product, without a cost-based justification.
A measure of how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in a product's own price.
A form of international price discrimination where a firm sells a product at a higher price abroad than in its home market.
A framework identifying Technical, Human and Conceptual skills as the components of managerial competence.
A rapid rate of inflation, roughly 10-20%, signalling an overheating economy.
Fayol's principle establishing a clear, unbroken line of authority from top management down to the lowest levels.
F.W. Taylor's approach of applying scientific methods — time and motion study, standardisation — to maximise shop-floor efficiency.
An unusual economic condition combining high inflation with high unemployment and stagnant growth.
A corporate governance theory viewing managers as trustworthy stewards of the company rather than self-interested agents.
A management perspective viewing the organisation as an open system of interdependent subsystems interacting with the external environment.
Taylor's technique of breaking tasks into steps, analysing movements and time, and setting output standards.
A contemporary management approach prioritising continuous improvement and customer satisfaction.
A rational-consumer assumption stating that if a consumer prefers A to B and B to C, they must also prefer A to C.
A core success factor of a Value-Based Organisation, built through consistent ethical conduct and shared values.
Fayol's principle that each employee should receive orders from only one superior, to avoid confusion.
Fayol's principle that one plan and one leader should guide all activities sharing the same objective.
An ethical decision-making approach favouring the action that provides the greatest good for the greatest number of people.
A method of measuring national income by summing the value created at every stage of production.
An organisation where ethical values shape culture, leadership and strategy, prioritising societal contribution alongside profit.
An ethical theory emphasising the moral character of the decision-maker — such as honesty and courage — rather than rules or outcomes.
The long-term aspirational direction guiding an organisation's future growth, forming the top tier of the VBO hierarchy.
A moderate rate of inflation, roughly 3-10%, that gradually erodes purchasing power over time.
A measure of inflation based on bulk/producer prices, excluding services.
